title: Volumes and persistent data
description: Choose the right Docker storage strategy for databases, uploads, and configuration, and understand the security implications of bind mounts, named volumes, and tmpfs.

data.text: Containers are ephemeral by design. When a container stops or is replaced, everything written to its writable layer disappears. Persistent storage lets containers keep data across restarts and replacements. Choosing the right storage type also has major security implications.

Docker provides three main ways to persist data: bind mounts, named volumes, and tmpfs mounts. Each is suited to different use cases, and the wrong choice can leak sensitive host files into containers or cause data loss during deployments.

cards.title: Bind mounts
cards.description: Mounts a specific file or directory from the host filesystem into the container.
pros: Useful for development config and source code
Visible to both host and container
cons: Tightly couples container to host filesystem
Host file permissions apply inside the container
Risk of overwriting host files if container process runs as root

cards.title: Named volumes
cards.description: Docker-managed storage that lives in a dedicated area of the host filesystem.
pros: Easy to back up and migrate
Better performance on Docker Desktop for macOS and Windows
cons: Harder to inspect directly on the host
Backup requires Docker CLI or API

cards.title: tmpfs mounts
cards.description: Stores data in host memory only. Data never touches the host disk.
pros: Data is never written to disk
Automatically removed when the container stops
cons: Data is lost when the container stops
Not suitable for anything that must survive a restart

data.text: Bind mounts are the most dangerous storage option from a security perspective. When you mount `/var/run/docker.sock` into a container, you give that container full control over the Docker daemon. When you mount the host filesystem root or sensitive directories such as `/etc`, a compromised container can read or modify host secrets.

data.title: Never mount the Docker socket in production
data.text: Mounting `/var/run/docker.sock` into a container is equivalent to giving that container root access to the host. Many CI/CD and automation tools request this mount, but it should be treated as a critical security exception with compensating controls.
Named volumes for databases and uploads

Named volumes are the recommended storage type for databases, file uploads, and any data that must survive container restarts. They are managed by Docker, work consistently across operating systems, and can be backed up with `docker run --rm -v <volume>:/backup alpine tar czf /backup/backup.tar.gz /data`.

data.title: PostgreSQL with a named volume
data.content: This Compose snippet creates a named volume for PostgreSQL data and exposes the database only to the API service.
data.code:
services:
  database:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    secrets:
      - db_password
    networks:
      - data
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp
      - /run/postgresql

volumes:
  pgdata:

networks:
  data:
    internal: true

secrets:
  db_password:
    file: ./secrets/db_password.txt

data.text: Docker volumes are owned by root on the host by default. When a container runs as a non-root user, it may not have permission to write to a newly created volume. Fix this by `chown`-ing the mount point in the Dockerfile or by using the `userns-remap` feature.

data.title: Volume permission guidelines
items: Set the correct ownership on the mount point in the Dockerfile with `RUN mkdir -p /data && chown appuser:appgroup /data`
Avoid running containers as root just to satisfy volume permissions
Use `docker volume inspect` to check volume mountpoints and driver options
Consider `userns-remap` for multi-tenant hosts to namespace UIDs

data.text: Use tmpfs mounts for sensitive temporary files such as decrypted secrets, session tokens, or database credentials that must exist only in memory. A tmpfs mount is never written to disk, so it cannot be recovered from a host disk image or forensic capture.

data.title: Using tmpfs for temporary runtime files
data.content: Mount a tmpfs volume at /tmp to keep temporary files in memory only.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Containers are ephemeral; use volumes for any data that must survive restarts
Named volumes are the safest default for databases and uploads
Avoid bind mounts for production data unless you need tight host integration
Never mount /var/run/docker.sock or sensitive host paths into production containers
Use tmpfs for sensitive temporary files that must never touch disk
data.takeaway: Persistent data should be isolated from the container runtime, secured with proper ownership, and backed up independently of the image.
